opus-5.5.text:
Well, first because it's happening anyway. Every student I have is using it, whether the syllabus allows it or not. So the question isn't whether they use it. It's whether we teach them to use it well or pretend it isn't there and let them figure it out alone, usually badly.

But the deeper reason is that I think we've been measuring the wrong thing for a long time. A lot of university assessment tests whether you can produce an artifact: an essay, a problem set, a summary of a paper. If a machine can now produce that artifact in ten seconds, then the artifact was never really the point. The point was the thinking behind it. AI forces us to admit that, and I think that's healthy.

In my own classes, I've flipped it. I tell students, "Use the AI. Generate the essay. Now tell me what's wrong with it. Where is it confidently incorrect? What question did it not think to ask?" That's a much harder task than writing the essay from scratch, and it's much closer to what they'll do in the real world. Nobody in a company is going to say, "Please don't use the tool." They'll say, "Use the tool, and be the person who knows when it's lying."

There's also a neuroscience angle I care about. The brain is lazy in a good way. It offloads whatever it can. We offloaded memory to writing, arithmetic to calculators, navigation to GPS. Each time people said it would make us dumber, and in some narrow ways it did. I can't remember phone numbers anymore. But it freed up resources for other things. The risk with AI is that we offload the thinking itself, the struggle that actually builds understanding. So universities have a real role here. Not banning the tool, but designing experiences where the struggle still happens, just at a higher level.

And honestly, the students are often ahead of us. If universities treat AI as cheating, they become irrelevant, because the students will learn the most important skill of their generation somewhere else. I'd rather we be the place where they learn it thoughtfully.

r001.rationale: The response says students are already using AI, so universities should teach them to use it well rather than leave them to figure it out alone.

r002.rationale: It compares AI with earlier tools that offloaded tasks, explicitly including calculators for arithmetic, while noting that AI can offload thinking itself.

fable-5.1.text:
Look, I'll give you the answer I give my students at Columbia, because I actually say this on the first day of class: I don't just allow you to use AI, I want you to use it. And people find that surprising coming from a professor, but to me the alternative is absurd.

Think about what we're actually doing when we ban it. We're saying, "There's a tool that every one of you will use the moment you walk out of this building, in every job you'll ever have, and for the next four years we're going to pretend it doesn't exist." That's not education, that's theater. We did the same thing with calculators, with Wikipedia, with the internet itself. Every time, the schools lost, and every time, the students who learned to use the tool well ended up ahead.

But the deeper reason, and this is the neuroscientist in me talking, is that the thing we were measuring was never the essay. The essay was a proxy. We wanted to know: can you think? Can you take an idea, pressure-test it, notice when something's wrong, change your mind? Now the proxy is broken, because a machine can produce the proxy in eleven seconds. So the honest response isn't to police the proxy harder. It's to admit it was always a proxy and go find a better way to measure the real thing.

And what I've found is that AI actually makes that easier, not harder. When a student brings me something an AI wrote, I ask them, "Why is this wrong?" Because it's always a little bit wrong. The model is confident, it's fluent, and it's missing something. And the student who can find what it's missing, that student has learned more than the one who wrote a mediocre essay alone at two in the morning. You're training the skill that matters now, which is judgment. Knowing when to trust the machine and when not to.

The last thing I'd say is, the universities that resist this are doing it out of fear, and fear is a terrible way to design a curriculum. The students aren't afraid. They're already using it. The only question is whether they're using it with us in the room or hiding it from us. I'd rather be in the room.

r001.rationale: The candidate says students will use AI in every future job and argues they should learn to use it well with universities involved.

r002.rationale: The candidate explicitly compares schools’ resistance to AI with their past resistance to calculators.

astra-6.text:
Because our job is to prepare students for the world they’re going to live in, and that world includes AI. If we teach them to solve problems only under conditions where AI doesn’t exist, we’re preparing them for an artificial environment.

That doesn’t mean we should stop teaching them to think. It means we have to be more thoughtful about what thinking we’re asking them to do. If a student can put my assignment into a machine and get a perfectly acceptable answer, maybe I need to change the assignment. Ask them to evaluate the answer, find the mistake, defend an assumption, or explain what evidence would change their mind.

There’s still a place for practicing without assistance. You need enough understanding to recognize when the machine is wrong. But banning the tool avoids the more interesting educational question: how do you teach someone to use it well, while remaining responsible for what they produce?

r001.rationale: The response says AI will be part of students’ future and argues universities should teach them to use it well.

r002.rationale: The response does not compare students’ use of AI to using a calculator.

sol-6.1.text:
Because the point of education should be to teach people how to think, how to ask good questions, and how to judge an answer. If a tool changes what students can do, we should change what we ask of them.

Imagine I give you an assignment and AI can answer it in ten seconds. We can spend all our energy trying to catch you using it, or I can ask a better question: “Here’s the AI’s answer. Where is it wrong? What assumptions did it make? How would you test its claims?” Now you have to understand the material.

There’s still a place for doing things yourself. You need enough knowledge to recognize when the machine gives you nonsense. But students are going to enter a world where these tools exist. A university should prepare them to use those tools thoughtfully, and to know when they shouldn’t trust them.

r001.rationale: The response says students will enter a world where these tools exist and universities should prepare them to use the tools thoughtfully.

r002.rationale: The response discusses AI tools in education but does not compare students’ use of AI to using a calculator.
